pages.summary: States why the book exists. Cubing resources lack annotations that say when to learn something, how much faster it makes you, what progression to expect and which resource is best. The Reader aims to be the missing 'user manual' that matches top-quality resources to skill level and sets expectations. In content it is an improvement guide and a curated resource collection combined, with the authors' opinions and answers to common FAQs.

pages.summary: Explains how to read the book. It assumes the reader knows beginner Roux and points to tutorial.rouxers.com for anyone who does not. It describes three ways to read: look up a topic (e.g. FB turning, EOLR progression), browse for something to learn, or check the FAQ. The book is organised by the four Roux steps (FB, SB, CMLL, LSE) plus generic chapters. Blockbuilding is split into solutions, fingertricks and lookahead, and each part has an overview of what a fast cuber does, a progression by skill level, then curated resources with commentary. CMLL and LSE follow the same pattern and add sub-step variants and algorithms. OH and 2H are covered together. The page also has contribution instructions (mdBook, pull request) and a roadmap frozen at v0.1, 'early phase as of Sept 22 [2020]'.

pages.summary: For general blockbuilding strategy it points to section 2.1 of an FMC tutorial (fmcsolves.cubing.net). It contrasts the two blocks. FB planning is static: you use inspection to craft an efficient solution. SB solving is dynamic: you track pieces in real time and may trade efficiency for fluency and lookahead. On orientation and colour neutrality, x2y (8 FB options, i.e. dual-colour) is 'highly recommended' because it is the smallest orientation that can use any premade pair. y or x2y2 (4 options) halve the odds of an easy case but are acceptable. Anything narrower is recommended against. Full CN (24 options) is unproven at world-class level, but it gives two last-pair choices for any first square; verdict: 'worth exploring, but don't force yourself'. A linked movecount statistics sheet shows x2y raises the chance of an easy first square from 60% (y) to 80%.
topics: FB static planning vs SB dynamic solving
drills: Expand your FB orientation to x2y; avoid anything narrower than y or x2y2

pages.summary: The most complete page. Step I covers the two FB families, square+pair (more common) and line+line, with links to strategy videos (teoidus, Louis' FB playlist, Iuri Grangeiro) and Kavin's beginner-friendly pair+pair and square+pair example solves. It defines planning as solution + tracking. FB pair piece relations: to solve a pair you need the edge's position and orientation, plus the corner's position and where its D-face sticker is. Worked examples are given, including pairing the DL edge with a corner for a D-line (R U R'). Step II covers improving solutions. Influencing: in two-stage solutions (square→pair, E-line→D-line), you either solve the first stage differently or add influencing moves, so that second-stage pieces end up better oriented or stay untouched. You predict where the uninfluencable piece lands, influence the other one within a moveset that leaves stage 1 intact, and accept that influencing is not always worth it. There are 17 worked influencing examples, each with an interactive 3D cube showing only the FB pieces. Other advice: optimise last-pair solutions, study example solves and text reconstructions (Kian, Alex, Sean on SpeedCubeDB, CubeSolves, r/rouxles), and develop 'taste' for good FB/FS. Turning: turn calmly and fluidly so you can track SB pieces, because the FB moveset (F/B) is hard to fingertrick. Plan fingertricks in inspection, limit regrips, and rank ergonomic pairs and triggers above raw movecount. Planning and tracking: plan FS first if the full FB is too much. To plan LP, compute the edge position/orientation and the corner position/D-sticker after FS. The four-step procedure is: stage-1 solution, then compute the stage-2 piece info, then try influencing with fingertricks in mind, then execute. Links go to onionhoney's tracking trainer and Kian's partial speed-BLD warmup.

pages.summary: Only the DR-first vs freestyle section is written. DR-first is used by most world-level Rouxers (Kian Mansour, Sean Villanueva). It simplifies tracking and pattern recognition, and most SB resources assume it. Freestyle (a superset) builds the second square any way, e.g. make a pair and insert the remaining edge, or insert any edge and then the remaining pair. It may be more efficient but demands more recognition and tracking, and is unproven as a standalone strategy. The recommendation for every level is DR-first as the default, with freestyle SS shortcuts used when easy patterns appear. The footnote explains why: DR-first is the only SS strategy that does not lock the SS. It leaves a choice between two pairs, which raises the chance of a good case and leaves room for influencing.

Introduces the Last 10 Pieces as CMLL + LSE. CMLL has only 42 cases, which the page offers as motivation to learn full CMLL now. Because the M slice is free, CMLL algs use r (Rw) moves for efficiency. LSE is 2-gen (M/U), which favours one-handed solving, and it is intuitive, so do not brute-force memorise it. A section on the CMLL→LSE transition says it is key for high-level solvers and promises to cover it.

pages.summary: Lays out a recognition progression 'from beginner's 4-tile to all angles'. Stage I, beginner (2-look CMLL): only corner orientation matters, so practise recognising it fast. Stage II, partial/full CMLL: colours matter. Know in advance which AUF angle shows the case (use U moves, not rotations), and peek by tilting the cube when you are 90 degrees off, which saves at least one move. This stage is fine up to sub-12, sub-10 or beyond. Stage III, all-angles recognition: H and Pi cases are effortless because all their colours show on top. For the other cases, infer hidden stickers from the facts that each side colour appears exactly twice across the four corners and only adjacent colours share a corner, and learn each case's colour pattern. An interactive worked example narrows a U case to the 'X' or 'Bottom Row' U case (SpeedCubeDB names) and then picks 'X' from the back-sticker inference. The page links Kian's 'How to Recognize CMLLs from All Angles'.

pages.summary: Two substantive sections, each with interactive cube animations. The first covers regular EOLRb insertions (3 cases) with verbal rules, e.g. 'M/M' to keep the LR edge on top, U2, then the opposite M'. The second is 'EOLRb 4C Non-Cycle Influencing' (8 cases). It starts once EO is solved and covers cases that would otherwise give a non-cycle 4c. Inserting the LR edges the non-standard way either skips dots (a 4c skip) or leaves a 2- or 3-move 4c (U2 M2 or M2 U2 M2) instead of a 5-mover (e.g. M' U2 M2 U2 M). Recognise these from U-face colours and pattern, and form your own recognition. Elsewhere, EOLR progression says not to memorise algsheets and to learn from text descriptions instead (two Google Docs, 'EOLR' and 'EOLR described', followed by a TODO asking how they differ).

pages.summary: Two questions. First, when to start full CMLL and EOLR: learn full CMLL as soon as possible, and start at the latest when averaging about 20-30 s. Learn EOLR only after full CMLL, ideally starting around a 15 s average. Second, how to improve blocks: study solves by fast Roux solvers (Kian, Sean, etc.), with explained example solves preferred over bare reconstructions, and look at how they plan and optimise for movecount and ergonomics. The page recommends Cubegrass Block Trainer (FB, SB, SS) and Zhouheng's/onionhoney's Roux Trainers (tough FB, FB solution generators for any block, Pair+DR, SS, tracking).

notes:
The Roux Reader is small and abandoned. Content commits stopped on 2022-01-15, the roadmap is still v0.1 (Sept 2020), and about half of the section headings are empty. Only fb, lse and cmll have substantial content, followed by blockbuilding, sb (DR-first vs freestyle only) and faqs. No glossary, appendix or exercise sets exist. Hardware, Beginner Resources, FB+DR and Switching are title-only, and the Switching link is a live 404.

Under MIT (Copyright (c) 2020 Rouxers) the substantive content can go straight into Rouxtine with attribution:
- 17 annotated FB influencing examples (full solutions plus explanations) and the FB-only stickering mask 'wttwttwtttttttttttrttrttttttttttttttbbbbbbtttttottottt'
- 3 regular EOLRb insertion patterns
- 8 EOLRb 4C non-cycle influencing / dots-skip cases
- a 3-stage CMLL recognition ladder
- the FB pair-relation rules
- milestone guidance: full CMLL by a 20-30 s average, EOLR after CMLL at about 15 s
- orientation advice: x2y recommended, CN optional
- DR-first as the default SB, with freestyle shortcuts
- the per-step 'overview → progression → resources' framework, split into solutions, fingertricks and lookahead

Feature ideas drawn from the book:
- FB influencing lesson and quiz: show the stage-1 solution and ask for the influencing move
- FB pair-relation drill: given the corner position and D-sticker, where can the edge go
- LP case trainer with untimed 'find another solution' mode
- FB 'taste' speed drill: rank the 8 x2y FB options quickly
- inspection fingertrick-planning prompt
- tracking trainer with partial speed-BLD warmup mode
- CMLL recognition trainer in three modes: orientation-only, fixed-angle with peeking, all-angles with hidden-sticker inference
- EOLRb insertion and 4c influencing trainer
- skill-level milestone hints

The stubs show topics the community wanted but nobody wrote, which the app could cover: SB pair progression and influencing, SB lookahead, the FB-SB transition, NMCMLL, FB+DR, CMLL alg resources for 2H and OH, CMLL turning, predicting CMLL from the SB last slot, predicting EO and LR from CMLL, CMLLEO / Pinkie Pie / L10P variants, 3-look vs EOLR progression, MC vs non-MC, EOBF, 4c recognition methods, LSE fingertricks for 2H and OH, hardware, and beginner resources.

Scope caution: L10P compares CMLL with CFOP's OLL+PLL, and one chapter is 'Switching from CFOP'. Both conflict with the Roux-only rule.

The interactive cubes use TwistySim v1.5.5. The Playwright render confirmed they work: 17 canvases on fb, 1 on cmll, 11 on lse, no JS errors.

This matches the earlier research (roux-training-features.md), which said 'book: MIT' and listed FB+DR, SB lookahead, CMLL prediction and 4c recognition as stubs; all confirmed. It adds that hardware, beginner resources, CMLL algs/turning, LSE progression/fingertricks and the CFOP switching page are also stubs.
